utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljkovic. I hope I haven't mangled your name.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Veljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Velibor and my last name is V-e-l-j-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: 19th November, 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand you are a police officer. Can you tell us briefly about your career in the police, when you started, what ranks you held, and what posts are the places you were stationed at.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I started working for the police as of 25th of April, 1994; and in the Secretariat of the Interior of Prizren and the police station in Suva Reka, I began working as of August 20th, 1994. And I remained there working until the withdrawal of all military and police forces from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please continue, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: After I arrived at the police station in Suva Reka, the first two years I was a beat policeman, maybe two or three shifts in the traffic control, and within the sector itself, but for the most part I worked as a beat police officer. After that, by decision of the commander of the station, I was involved in misdemeanours. In other words, I entered information on misdemeanours involving traffic accident into a computer and then later on once a court decision was issued, I would also enter that in the computer database and basically that was my work. As of 1997 by the decision of the same commander, together with another colleague I was in charge of the station records. I attended a course to be able to do this, and I remained in this position until we withdrew from Kosovo. Whereas the colleague who worked with me, pursuant to a decision by the commander, he was involved in special missions in the field and he only came to do -- he was only involved in work relating to the police records when I was away or over the weekends. And this was when the police -- when the attacks against the police began in 1998. And I remained in this job until 11 June, 1999, until the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are at the withdrawal, can you tell us what happened to the records of the Suva Reka police station at the time when you withdrew in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: A few days prior to the withdrawal and during a break in the air-strikes, the police station commander told me that all the papers, all the documents from previous years, I mean, the years up until 1998, that I should destroy all those records. So I went to the station and all these records that really I selected, not him because he wasn't there any more, I selected the papers that I felt should be destroyed and I took them and burnt them. And as for the documentation and records of 1998 and 1999, I packed them and loaded them on a truck which arrived a little later and took them away when -- at the time when we withdrew to Krusevac. Now, what happened with the archives and the files in Krusevac, I really wouldn't know. Whether they were just archived or destroyed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us who was the commander of the station in 1999 and what is his name? You just mentioned that you received orders from him.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Suva Reka police station as of June 1996 until the moment of withdrawal was Radojko Repanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recall the names and ranks of the other senior persons at the police station at that time and the jobs that they were tasked with?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the only higher position was the chief of station. There were no other senior ranks in Suva Reka itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was the chief of station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the station was Dobrivoje Vitosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what is the difference between the chief of station and the commander of the station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the station was in charge of the civilian aspect, in other words, the administrative work and crime prevention. Whereas the station commander, together with his deputy and assistants, was in charge of duties relating to the uniform police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which section were you a part of, the administrative or the uniform police?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- my post was administrative, and although I did administrative work, I did wear a uniform and I was in charge of the schedules of the police officers who were on patrol and so on, and I also supervised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of the deputies and their assistants to the station commander Mr. Repanovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: We only had one deputy and one assistant commander. The deputy's name was Dragan Borisavljevic, whereas the assistant commander was Nenad Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a PJP unit attached to the Suva Reka police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. Within the Suva Reka police station there were only employees who had regular posts at the Suva Reka police station and who were members of the PJP by -- pursuant to a decision of the commander, but later on there were also some men who were attached from other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if Nenad Jovanovic had any association or position in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about that. He was more involved with members of the reserve force, police force, and preparing monthly reports, which would contain the working hours and the outcome of different assignments. As for the special unit, the PJP, I really couldn't say anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there members of the DB, and by that I mean the department of state security, at Suva Reka police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were, but we were in the same building but they had a separate entrance and exit, so these members of the DB had a special office, a separate office. Now, how their work was organised and what the delineation of work between the police officers and the DB officers was, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not there was cooperation or lack of cooperation with the DB officers and the officers from the department of public security?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the -- who was the commander of the DB personnel that were at the station in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall. I don't know who their officer was -- their chief was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall a particular day - I don't know if I should lead you to the dates, I'll ask you to recall the date - in Suva Reka when a significant amount of Albanian people were killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 26th of March, 1999. That was the first -- so when I was questioned for the first time by our men at the ministry in Belgrade, when asked about the day when a lot of people were killed, I could not recall the date. And then they told me -- they asked me if I could remember approximately what the weather was like. I know -- or what the time was, and they told me that at the time we were still at the station, we hadn't moved out, withdrawn. I think this was -- and then I told him that I thought this was in the first -- during the first week of the air-strikes, and then they confirmed that and told me that, yes, it was on the 26th of March, 1999. So when we know that the air-strikes began on the 24th of March, 1999, then that means that I was about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall or did you discover the family name of persons in a large group of those Kosovar Albanians who were killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the family you are asking me about, I know where the house was. This was at the house in Suva Reka at Restanksi Put. On Restanksi Put Street, I think there was no number, no street number. It was on the right-hand side of the road from the direction of Suva Reka towards Pecane.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Do you remember the family name? Did you get to discover the family name of some of the people who were killed on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was only told. I didn't know who the family was, but during the interview, the first interview, I was told that it was the family Berisha, the killing of the Berisha family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, that morning, the morning of the 26th of March, 1999, about what time did you arrive? Well, did you go to work at the police station that day, and if so, about what time did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I slept in the building which was on the same compound where the police station was in Suva Reka. The sleeping quarters were on the same premises, within the same compound where I worked. It was about 5 to 6 metres from my office. My working hours were from 7.00 to 3.00 p.m.; but because of the air-strikes, I remained on the premises of the police station, which is to say that on that day, on the 26th of March, 1999, I arrived around 7.00 at the office and opened it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the morning, that morning, was there an incident which occurred in the courtyard outside the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Later on in the day or at any time in the day, was there an incident that occurred in the courtyard of the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the day, I think around noon, yes, there was an incident. Maybe a little earlier or a little later, but about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what you saw and what you heard when that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of March around 12:00 noon, I left the building where I was working because the schedule was only done formally. So there was about 10 to 15 minutes of work for me there. I locked up the office and decided to go and sit with the colleagues at the duty office, duty station, which was in Suva Reka. Unaware of what was about to happen, I just ran into trouble. When I came to the station itself, I found my colleague Sladjan Cukaric, Radovan Tanovic, Miroslav Petkovic there, they were at the very entrance to the OUP building and with them was Commander Repanovic. The colleagues that I mentioned, Sladjan Cukaric, Radovan Tanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I'm just going to ask you to mention those names again, to repeat them, but a little bit more slowly this time.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The colleagues were Sladjan Cukaric, Radovan Tanovic, they were members of the active duty force. And there was also Miroslav Petkovic, he was a member of the reserve police. The three of them were at the very entrance of the Suva Reka police station. They had automatic rifles and flak jackets. The commander Radojko Repanovic was also there. Just as I was getting ready to enter the Suva Reka OUP building, Commander Repanovic told me, I can't recall the exact words, but I figured that what he had told me was, in fact, a criminal offence. He told me to go with the colleagues that I -- whose names I mentioned, somewhere. I don't recall what I replied, but I just refused. I simply refused to go with him and entered the premises of the duty operations room. And he, as my superior, did not say anything else after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you continue, I'm sorry to interrupt you, I just want to clarify something and to tell us as best as you can from memory, did he tell you to go and do anything and why did you figure that what he told you was a criminal offence? Just tell us what he said you were to do, from the best of your memory.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you something first, I can't recall what he said exactly. Over the four statements I gave, I told everyone questioning me that I can't recall. In any way, I realised that following through that -- with that order would constitute an offence or a breach of work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What offence?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The crime of murder. It would be the gravest breach of work duty. When one fires a weapon, it is very easy to kill someone or disable them for the rest of their life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well then, we'll return to that. Let's continue the narrative. He told you to go, and you refused to go with them; you went into the police station. What happened after that? Sorry, you went into the OUP building, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I think I sat on a chair that was next to the person in charge of the duty officer at that point in time. Although I cannot remember who that person was. A lot of time has passed. I can't tell you who was there at the duty office. I simply sat down in the room where we kept those detained. There had been a person brought in two or three days prior to that. He was suspected of carrying out an armed attack against a patrol. I saw that man. In my view, he was between 50 and 60 years of age. His height was around 1Dusa0 centimetres and some 90 kilos of weight. He was balding. What was left of his hair was grey. He wore a sweater. It was white with a black pattern. He had black pants. He was brought in as a suspect. I don't know which part of the Suva Reka territory they found him. Under the law, one of the reasons for bringing in a person without an order was if that person was caught in the process of committing a crime. That is to say, the attack on the police. They brought him a few days prior to that, and it was unknown what would happen with him. I don't know who had the key of the detention room at that time. In any case, he was eventually taken out of the station building. I don't remember who took him out. In any case, they took him out and brought him to the courtyard. Less than half a minute later, I heard shots from a fire-arm, although I don't know which fire-arm it was. I don't know if it was an automatic rifle or the CZ-99 handgun. I heard several shots, I believe. When I came out of the building, I saw him dead in the courtyard. Next to him in the courtyard was Sladjan Cukaric, Radovan Tanovic, and Miroslav Petkovic; they were all there. Which one of them shot him dead, is something I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from what you are saying, they had weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is a bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: My work-mates?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those that you saw in the vicinity of this man who had been shot.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. As I told you, they had an automatic rifle and a CZ-99 handgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what time did this occur?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 12:00 and 12.10. He was killed in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this before or after Commander Repanovic told you to go with the men?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was right after that. Perhaps it all took place within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what ethnicity was this man who had been shot in the courtyard of the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: He was Albanian. I didn't know his name at the time. But when I was being questioned by the investigative judge, he told me that that person's name was Petrit Elshani. Up to that point, I didn't know this person's first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after that? Did you remain there, did your colleagues remain there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you have in mind? Did you want to ask me whether my work-mates were sent elsewhere or whether they remained in the station yard? Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. When you went out into the courtyard and you saw this man who had been shot dead there, tell us what happened after you arrived there and saw what you saw.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Some 10 minutes later, Radovan Tanovic as well as Sladjan Cukaric and Miroslav Petkovic, who was a reservist, simply left. They went towards Cara Dushana Street; I can't recall exactly in which direction they left. Whether they went towards Recani or Pecane, or in the direction of Prizren, this is something I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after they left, did you hear sounds indicating that anything was occurring in the area of Suva Reka? The town of Suva Reka, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: After the murder of Petrit Elshani, I was in the courtyard of the police station and then I went inside and sat in the duty service room, after having seen the three of my work-mates leave. Some ten minutes later in close vicinity, I heard shots from an automatic rifle which came from the direction of Pecane. I wanted to go out to see from which house the shots were coming. It occurred to me that perhaps a family was being killed. I was out on the pavement in Cara Dushana Street which is as one exits the police station yard in Suva Reka where there was always the vehicle of the intervention patrol parked. I saw a house perhaps 100 metres away from the Suva Reka police station being on fire. I saw people running away from the house, some of whom were falling dead. I simultaneously heard those automatic rifle shots being fired. Those who were not hit crossed Restanksi Put and entered the yard of the bus station still running. In the courtyard of the bus station there is also a shopping centre, and I thought that some of them were trying to find refuge in any of the shops. In front of the station there was a vehicle, but I can't remember its registration plates, which had arrived from the direction of Prizren. I saw some people in the yard of that house. There may have been five or six of them. They were dead. Although I observed that from a distance of about 100 metres, I could still clearly see that. I can't remember who it was that told me to start loading up the corpses. It was a logical thing to do, that those people had to be buried, otherwise contamination occurs and there may be an outbreak. I was told, in any case, to go and load the corpses --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I picked up my automatic rifle from the admin office. I took my side-arm. I can't remember whether I already had it on me or whether I picked it up at the same time I did the rifle from the office. In any case, I set out with two other -- with two reservists. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) We picked up the corpses. I think we picked up the man who was in the yard first. I then I started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since we have paused here, Mr. Veljkovic, I'm going to ask you to just give us a couple of more details from the narrative you just gave. You had reached a point where you set off with other reservists to collect the bodies. You said the shots you heard while you were in the police station came from automatic rifles which came from the direction of Pecane. Where is Pecane?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Pecane is about 3 to 4 kilometres from the territory of Suva Reka. When I was explaining what took place, I wanted to designate the direction of two of the closest settlements, that's why I said Pecane, although it's not all that close from Suva Reka. In any case, it's not too far either. It was still within the territory of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you say it come from the direction of Pecane, about how far away, can you estimate, the sounds of those gun-shots came from?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, when I came -- well, first of all, I was in the building when I heard the shots. When I came outside, one could hear the shots even better. Then I saw those people falling down, being killed, and the house was already on fire. Then it occurred to me that an Albanian family is being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you see who was or were firing these shots when you came out of the station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I could not see that. I could only hear the shots but not who fired them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said you saw people running away from the house, can you describe these people? Were they -- by sex, age, or were they civilian or military? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I came there, I saw that these were only civilians. They were not military personnel. They had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were their approximate ages and sex of these people?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, from the distance where I was, I couldn't exactly see how old they were and of what gender; but when I went to the pizzeria where they were killed, I saw that some children were there as well, perhaps 5 or 6 years old, some were 12 or 15 years old. There were also women and some men there. In any case, it was predominantly women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: They were Albanian. I subsequently learned that this was the Albanian family Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us also that you can't remember who it was who told you to start loading up corpses. Where were you when you were told that you should go and start loading corpses?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but I think I was just outside the Suva Reka police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said there was a truck that arrived from Prizren, I believe you said. Did you use a truck in the process of loading the bodies?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, Petrit Elshani was put onto the truck, and then together with my two work-mates I went towards the Berisha family home to load the corpses there. I can't recall who the driver was. I don't think he was from the territory of Suva Reka. The three of us were on foot following the truck which drove slowly. Once by the corpses we simply loaded them onto the trailer of that truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many bodies in front of that house?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, although I spoke about that at the time when my work-mates testified in this case as well. I'm also using some information that I heard on the Serbian TV. I think there were five or six of them, and I believe my work-mates confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I want you to be clear with us, make a clear distinction between something that you might have discovered or you were told and something that you saw and observed otherwise directly yourself, please. After you loaded those bodies in the -- from in front of the house, the Berisha family home, where next did you travel to and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: We went in the direction -- well, one comes across two villages following that road: To the right one goes to Pecane, and if you continue straight on you reach Studencani. We went towards Studencani. It was inconceivable to reach Studencani by that time, let alone enter it. But in any case, at some point on the road, the driver turned the truck and we went back to the Suva Reka police station. As we were moving towards Studencani, I heard a hand-grenade explode. I don't know which hand-grenade exactly, what type, since I'm not an expert in that. The sound came from the direction of Restanksi Put, somewhere from the area of the Metohija Vino winery and where the municipal hall is as well as the defence Secretariat. Perhaps after the detonation itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you travelled from the police station towards the place where the truck turned around, did you and your two colleagues from the reserve do anything? What were you doing as you travelled in the truck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: We loaded those five or six bodies and then went towards Studencani. Whether there were any other corpses further up the road away from the house is something I cannot recall. Maybe there were some corpses there of people who had been killed earlier, in any case, I cannot say anything precisely. We went up the road to a certain point where we turned back. I'm telling you that there were five or six corpses on that truck that we loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who organised the truck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. Actually, I don't know. The true answer is that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened when you returned to the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I simply returned towards the police station when I heard that explosion from the Metohija vino company. I also heard automatic rifle gun-shots. After that, I went in the direction of the gun-shots because I was -- I presumed that the people who had fled the house wanted to hide in a shop. They did so, but that presented them with no refuge. I went to see where they were killed, still hoping that they were not, that they were alive. I went along Cara Dushana Street with the two work-mates, and I apologised for having disclosed one of their names. No one told me previously whether anyone was a protected witness or not. I was moving in that direction to see whether the people were killed and whether they needed to be loaded on to the truck. When I was some 30 to 40 metres away next to the gas station, I saw some people. I can't remember all who was there, but I realised that the family members were killed in one of the nearby shops. As I came close to the pizzeria, I think it had opened two or three years before that and was only 10 metres away from the main street, Cara Dushana Street. As I came close, I saw some people there, and I'll only tell you about those that I'm certain of. It was Tanovic, Cukaric, and Petkovic who were standing outside the pizzeria in front of the door. When I saw that, I realized those people were killed. I approached the door and I saw dead people. From where I stood, I could see that these were predominantly women, children, and a few men. That's it. Then we simply started loading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they all dead or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were dead. Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you saw these people in the pizzeria, you said: "When I saw that, I realised these people were killed. I approached the door, and I saw dead people." What I want to know is: Every body inside that pizzeria you saw was dead when you first stepped in?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: At my first impression, they were dead. And in my view, they were all dead. Whether they actually all were dead or not, I can't really recall, but in my view they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said "we simply started loading them." While you were loading them, did any body speak?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody said a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall if any of the Albanians inside that pizzeria that you thought was dead spoke or moved?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I began loading the bodies onto the truck, I can't recall exactly how much time passed, but there was a woman lying by the door. And during my first interview in Belgrade in late February 2003, I was told she was wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just tell us for the time being exactly what you saw or heard while you were in the pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I had loaded a few bodies and there was a woman by the door, I thought she was dead. She was about 65 to 70 years old. She wore the Albanian-style pants, and she said something to me in Albanian, although I can't speak Albanian, and she reached out with her arm. And then I saw that one of her arms, I can't recall which one it was, that she was wounded in the arm. And then she said something to me and I was startled and I had both a rifle and a pistol on me. I had left the rifle by the door and then I was startled when I realised that she was alive. I picked up the rifle, and I think I said, Oh, she is alive; when one of my colleagues entered the pizzeria, fired a shot, and killed the woman. So in fact, that woman was slightly wounded at the time and she would have survived but then she was shot and killed. I cannot say who fired and who shot her execution style in the pizzeria, but then I just continued loading the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean you cannot say who fired? You can't recall or you don't know the person or you didn't see the person who fired? Would you like to go into private session to say who fired, if you can?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really say. I can't say who shot her. I simply cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were laying down in the pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: When this woman was shot dead, I continued loading the bodies. And then after awhile, I can't say exactly how much time later, I saw a man whom I knew. He was about 35 to 40 years old. He was dressed in black. He had a dark complexion, black hair. He was about 6 feet tall, about Dusa0 kilos, and I know that he was a bus driver. He just said -- I saw him actually getting up to his feet and he said, You've shot my entire family dead. Spare me at least. I left the room again and again somebody entered the pizzeria, fired a shot, and killed the man. And I can't recall who it was who shot him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you load these bodies from the pizzeria on the same truck that you had travelled with to on the Restanski Put Road or was there another truck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we loaded all the bodies onto the same truck where we loaded the bodies from the Restanksi Put. I don't think that another vehicle came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The loading of the bodies from the pizzeria, was that supervised by anybody?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there were people from the Suva Reka -- from the Suva Reka utility company, he came, and then I think Dr. Boban Vuksanovic came -- arrived later. He was the director of the medical centre. I don't know if he was there when I arrived, but I think he came later. And they too helped with the loading of the bodies. And then I realised that this was a horrible incident. There were, I don't know exactly how many bodies, I just went to the compound, the police station courtyard. I didn't want to load the bodies any more, and I think that the people from the funeral home or the utilities company, public utilities company, came and they continued loading on the bodies. And it was impossible at the time to just leave and go to Pristina because there were terrorists attacking from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know you will not be able to tell us precisely how many bodies were in the pizzeria, but can you just give us an approximation, a sort of ball-park figure as to how many bodies you saw in the pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, during the interviews, and I was interviewed on a number of occasions, and when I made my statement before the deputy public Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just tell us what you remember. We will look at those if we need to refresh your memory. But for the time being, tell us what you remember in terms of the amount, the approximate amount of bodies that were there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say, and maybe I'm wrong, that there were about 100 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the pizzeria now, about how many from the pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about that number. In my assessment, about 90 to 100 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we just have an look at an aerial photograph of the area. We are not going to go through all of what you told us, sir, but just to point out one or two places to -- so we could understand the narrative more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is 50 -- sorry, 05337.01. That's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you arrange yourself -- oh, that's a marked map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a map marked by the witness. I don't know if that would be -- if we should start with an unmarked map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be better if the witness marked a fresh map, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we replace this with D13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's start by -- if you can be given a marker or a pen. If you could put a circle around the SUP and OUP building. Before you start drawing, just identify them where they are in your mind first and then put a circle around them. Can you do that? Do you see them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the SUP and the OUP, that's one in the same thing. I will mark it now. The main police station building and also the other -- the other buildings in the compound. Do you want me to just mark the main building or also the auxiliary facilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just mark the main police building.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you put a number 1 at the place you were standing at when you first saw the bodies running from the house and running from the vicinity of Restanksi Put. That is, the place where you were at when you first saw these civilians running away.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to put number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you put a number 2 on the house or immediately in front of the house that you saw these people running from?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately here, although I've already marked it by putting 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is the house? Which one is the house? Just put an X on the house, if you can.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you put just the initials RS on the street that you refer to as Restanksi Put. Just, if you can, put RS, the initials, on the street that you refer to as Restanksi Put. Or, let me ask first, where is that street in relation to the number 2?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's in this area between all these houses and the bus-stop. So the vehicles that you see, the parked vehicles, that is in fact Restanksi Put, and where the sign is, that is the intersection or the very beginning of Restanksi Put Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So where the 2 is at, where you said you saw the people running, that is Restanksi Put?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you just draw an arrow on that street to indicate the direction that you travelled on the truck after you picked up the bodies, the five bodies. Just an arrow on the street on Restanksi Put pointing in the direction that you travelled with the truck.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where, if you could tell us, did you pick up the five or so bodies?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the stop where I put number 2, approximately there. But the bodies were not on the road itself, rather, they were some five or six metres away. Whether this was the property -- on the property of the Berisha family or whether this was just public ground, I really couldn't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how far along Restanksi Put did you travel before you turned back?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was a 15 minute ride or maybe a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately. I understand one can't tell the exact distance. Approximately how many metres or kilometres do you think you travelled up to the point where you turned back?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: About a kilometre, a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while you were travelling up to the road junction that you turned back on, did you see anything or anyone on the road?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. You mean whether I saw anyone alive or heaven forbid some dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Dead bodies in particular, since you mentioned it. Did you see any dead bodies further along Restanksi Put?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think there were any, but I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I can't really say for sure. But my answer is: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you travelled along Restanksi Put after having loaded the five bodies onto the truck, did you travel in the truck or did you walk behind the truck as you indicated you had been doing previously?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Both on the way out and on the way back I was on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the way back, did you load anything onto the truck or did any of your colleagues do so?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the way back, no. I know for certain that we -- I didn't on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you returned to the police station with the truck, how many bodies were on the truck?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was sure that these were only the people from the area that I marked with number 2. And when I returned, when I came back, I just went in that direction. I did not enter the premises of the OUP, but I just went on to the pizzeria. I've already explained that. Now, after that, when there were a few bodies left, I went to the police station on my own and other men stayed back to load the remaining bodies and they went to Prizren and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that while you were on your way back with the truck on Restanksi Put, you heard the sound of a grenade exploding and it seemed to be coming from the Metohija Vino. Can you see the Metohija Vino warehouse here, and if so, could you mark it with a number 3?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it here, and I've marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you mark the vicinity where the pizzeria is or the place where the pizzeria is with a small number 4. Just identify it in your mind first and then mark it with a small 4.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that building that you marked, what looks to me like an M or?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is this building, green, and here I can also see the petrol station, and this is the building close to the petrol station where there was an employee working, so it's some 15 metres away. The first cafe on the right-hand side on the Cara Dushana Street, that's the pizzeria so it was there, and then there was also the bus station and some other companies. I don't know exactly who the owners were. So this is what I marked, and I realised that in fact this looks like an M rather than a number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, very well. The green building, which -- what building did you say that was?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that pizzeria, that very pizzeria where the people were killed, I think that's the building. Whether this was owned by the Berisha family or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- you mentioned the first cafe on the right-hand side of a street. What is the name of the street you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The cafe was on Cara Dushana Street on the right-hand side viewed from Suva Reka towards Prizren. Or from Prizren to Suva Reka, it's on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is in that cafe?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That facility, that cafe, there were just tables and chairs and a bar. It was not a large cafe. Maybe 20 to 30 square metres, not bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that cafe the same as the pizzeria or where was it in relation to the pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the same. One in the same. I referred to it as a pizzeria and then as a cafe or rather a catering establishment. So that is the catering establishment I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you put a number 5 - because I'm not sure I understand - a number 5 at the place where this cafe is on Cara Dushana Street on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You marked that number 5 over the number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if we approached a convenient time? If we are there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have the first break now. Now, this exhibit needs to be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P01070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I said, we will have the first break now, and we resume at 11.00. The court officer will give you guidance during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from those people who were killed that day, can you tell us what happened in respect to the other Albanians who were living in Suva Reka on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from the pizzeria, I heard from someone that the order was that those competent within the ministry from Belgrade ordered that the killing should cease, and that the Albanians were to be told that they had to leave the territory of Suva Reka within half an hour, otherwise that they would meet the fate of the Berisha family. When I heard that, I was in the police station building in Suva Reka when the phone rang, the land-line of the duty service, and an Albanian woman was on the other end. I cannot repeat her words verbatim, but she asked what was this all about. We were told that we had to leave. I told her that, indeed, they had to leave. She asked me where to, and I told her to Albania. She asked me, What are we going to do in Albania? I didn't want to continue this conversation. I simply said, Go to Albania; you have to leave otherwise you will suffer the fate of the other ones. People who were nearby heard the firing in the Berisha compound and everyone knew what had taken place. I hung up and within half an hour there was an en masse departure of the members of the Albanian community by vehicles. They all went towards Prizren and Albania. As of that moment, there was no more killing. People simply left. We resumed our work. Two or three days later, we abandoned the police station in Suva Reka and we relocated to different locations. The bombardment stopped. We left Kosovo and never went back to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said someone told you that the order was for the Kosovar Albanians to leave. Was that person a policeman or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I think I heard that from my work-mates, although I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were you when you heard it?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, in the police station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the houses of the Kosovar Albanians in the Suva Reka area, did anything -- was anything done to these houses or to some of them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Along Restanski Put Road, I know that some Albanian houses were set on fire. Those behind the station were not. People packed their basic belongings and left. Whether the rest of their property was subsequently looted is something I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the killings that occurred that day, do you know whether any investigation was conducted into these murders at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I didn't hear of any investigation from the colleagues. As for the rest, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, you were not able to recall what precisely Mr. Repanovic, the station commander, told you to do and I'm wondering if I could, with the leave of the Court, remind you of what you said on a previous occasion and ask you if that refreshes your memory as to what Mr. Repanovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, may I just put to him something from his statement and ask him if he remembers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The more appropriate course would be to show the witness the statement and allow him to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But before we come to that point, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Your Honour. I think firstly we should put to the witness what Mr. Stamp has in mind and then show any documents. Mr. Stamp referred to something, but it is unknown what order by Commander Repanovic he had in mind. First, he should state his position to the witness and then show him the statement, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, the witness should be allowed to read any relevant part of his statement and then see whether or not that refreshes his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I, with the assistance of the usher, just hand him a copy of his signed statement and the translation into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, there is one statement there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic -- I'm so sorry. I will try not to flip the pages while the microphone is on, but it needs to be on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you look at the statement which is signed, there's a signed copy there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's your signature?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a signature of mine on every page. I can't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you go to the translation -- could you look this way, please. In B/C/S, sorry in Serbian, have a look at paragraph 16. Paragraph 15. And I'll just read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The highlighted part?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you read all of paragraph 15. Just read it.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: "A bit later I was in the police station and heard that Commander Repanovic addressed a group of policemen in a small room. I saw that the following were present: Shift leader, Milovan Gogic; Sladjan Cukaric; Radovan Tanovic; reservist, Ivica Novkovic; Ramiz Papic; and several other reservists whose names I cannot recall. The deputy commander was not present. He was out in the field. The assistant Jovanovic was not present and Vitosevic was in the building but in his own office. Repanovic told the men in the room that they were to go from house to house and kill the Albanian civilians. He did not say why this was to be done and he did not specify any particular individuals. He just said that they were all to be killed. Repanovic ordered me to go with them and take part in the killing but I refused. Repanovic did not say anything when I refused the order." Is that the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the 15th paragraph. Let me tell you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wait. Before you do, can I just ask you if you recall whether or not this is what happened, if that refreshes your memory as to what happened in the police station that morning?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain a few things to you now, and it is up to you whether you will accept it or not. Given that I signed each of the pages of the statement given at Jevrem Grujica Street, number 11, in Belgrade, on the 18th of January, 2006; this was the forced statement. In all forced statements, I relied on my memory, or the idea of events, as well as on the interjections of the people questioning me. That was also a problem at the main hearing in Belgrade. I referred to three people, and in the statement there are no longer three but ten people. Then the judge asked me what about the other seven? The people who interrogated me were very familiar with the case itself. In this paragraph, for example, I said that I was in front of the police station in Suva Reka and came across the people I referred to, without going into the names again. However, the person interviewing me would say, In addition to those people, there were this and that one. And I mentioned Cukaric Tanovic and Petkovic as well as my commander Repanovic. And then I was told by them, by the interviewers, that on top of those there were some other people and we learned from other witnesses that this was so, that Gogic was present at the meeting as well as the rest. And then I said I have to trust the interviewer. I can't say, You know what, you are lying because those people were not there. I can't do that. And then I said, If other witnesses said that these people were in attendance, then you could include them in my statement. And then what was combined or joined was my statement as well as the statement of other witnesses. Well, without going into any details, but I did undergo certain unpleasant things because their relatives would tell me, On top of these you mentioned this and that person. And then at the main hearing, I decided to tell exclusively what I thought was true and to explain why some of the statements did not tally. When I explained that, the presiding judge in Belgrade said to tell them what you saw, what I saw, rather than what I was told by others. And then I told them my idea of the events referring to what others said as well. Realistically speaking, the other witnesses had no reason to blame anyone without a sound basis. This is as far as the 15th paragraph goes. I do stand by my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You told us earlier when you testified that Mr. Repanovic told you to go. All I'm asking now is: Do you remember, having read that, what he told you and the other policemen to go and do?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking about a written order. I'm asking about events as they transpired that morning. And I'm asking you about what Mr. Repanovic said to the police officers who were gathered that morning. And all I'm asking you is: Do you recall whether or not Mr. -- or let me rephrase that question. Do you remember what Mr. Repanovic told you and the men to go out to do?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the morning, I can't recall whether I entered the station in Suva Reka in the auxiliary building. I can't say whether I heard from him or from any other work-mate of mine about the morning order. By the time I left at noon, I've already explained to you who it was that I came across at the entrance of the police station. I cannot recall the order itself exactly. It may strike you as illogical, but I realised that the order was illegal, therefore I refused to carry it out. Under the law, as an employee, I was duty-bound to refuse to carry out an illegal order. However, if an order is legal, then -- and I still refuse, then there are consequences to bear. I could be fired. In any case, the superior would be duty-bound to sanction such behaviour. Someone can tell me to bring in a person or do something else which would fall under --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, maybe I wasn't precise enough, so I'm going to be very precise. This statement that you gave, it was read back to you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what you just read here is that Mr. Repanovic told the men in the room that they were to go from house to house and kill the Albanian civilians. Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. Some people interviewing me told me that another witness had said that, and then I replied that if another witness said that then it might be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to that same issue, do you recall that you -- you were interviewed by the war crimes judge Milan Dilparic and that transcript was taken of the interview and this was on the 5th of March, 2004. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was on the 5th of March, 2004, where the interview was recorded. An audio recording was made. I answered the questions asked. Although, I was rather frightened and you can see that from the answers that I provided because I would repeat the same answer up to ten times and so that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement that is here at issue was a statement made to the investigators of the ICTY, and I did not see any other statements on this 65 ter list. And I -- so I wouldn't -- I don't know, and I wonder if they may be used. This is just a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a statement in 2006. As I understand the evidence of the witness, his reason for things being in this statement is that he had been interviewed earlier than 2006 in Belgrade and he had given evidence before an investigating judge in Belgrade before 2006. And that things that appear in this statement are not his recollection but what was put to him by those who interviewed him in Belgrade. That's how we get to the other statements. It is the witness's explanation for the contents of this statement. So carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have the transcript here, and it is difficult to use, but, Your Honours, can I just read the relevant part of the transcript to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of what transcript, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The transcript of what I just described. An interview in Belgrade in 2004 before the war crimes judge Dilparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How do we reach that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is your witness examination-in-chief. It's one thing to show him something to ask whether it refreshes his memory and if that's solely what you are doing ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. I have no intentions of crossing him. I just want to remind him of something he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to read something from your transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is page 5 and 6 in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you better have the witness confirm that he gave evidence or he was interviewed. I'm not clear yet which it is that you are dealing with. On a certain date and a certain situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you told me that you recall being interviewed in 2004, the 5th of March, 2004, by the war crimes judge Milan Dilparic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And a transcript was taken of the interview. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In fact, it was audio recorded?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to read to you the transcript from the record that I have and ask you basically if that helps to remember what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the B/C/S of the transcript, it's not paginated, but it is at the evidence registration number K040-8554, for the benefits of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Question by the investigating judge: "Tell me, you said in this report that you know that there was an order to go from door to door and kill Albanians in Suva Reka. Who gave that order?" Your answer was: "The order was given first by superior officers so I got it from them." You were asked: "From whom did you personally hear it?" And you said: "From -- from -- the order was from the station commander Radojko Repanovic and he said he probably -- and he did not make decisions or the station commander only and for the rest." You were asked: "How did he tell you this?" And you said: "You see that day when there were killings," I mean, he said: "Go there, load, and kill. And even a few days before that there were killings. But I do not know how he had said that, he must have said go from house to house and kill, probably something to that effect." Then you were asked: "Did he say this in front of you when you heard him say it?" And you said: "I didn't hear that when he said it but when I saw people go kill and him standing and watching quietly, I mean dead people being loaded, ones were killing the others were loading, I mean, well, now I heard that this order had come from Belgrade." So do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if this was audio recorded that means that no transcript was taken. And if it was audio recorded, then that would mean that that's what I said. Although, I began, as I've told you already, I was rather frightened during this audio recording. And I got confused. And as time went on, I have also begun to forget things. And I fear that maybe some of my presumptions may lead to some people being held to account, but it is true what I said there. I've signed the transcript, the audiotape is there. If it's not here, it's in Belgrade for sure. And I do stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection, but could I just have the page number because the one that was given K040-8554 does not exist. It starts -- the whole document begins with K040-8556.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I could hand a copy to counsel. This might be a better copy that starts from 8551. I think that will -- this is a copy that was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This was a matter of disclosure to the Defence. We didn't know how we would anticipate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's not in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are saying, Mr. Veljkovic. So there was some confusion. So later on the investigating judge - and this is page 29 in the English and K040-8560 in the B/C/S. He said: "I'm asking you one more time, are you sure that is Radojko Repanovic told you and go and kill everybody who is alive and to collect the dead?" And you said: "I am sure. I was in front of him when he said, Come on, you go as well as to load them." Having heard what I've just read of the transcript, can you tell us if you -- or what you recall that Radojko Repanovic said that morning?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only stand by what I've already said, what I heard from him, but I can't say what order he issued. I can only tell you about what I heard him say on that day after noon, after 12:00. But I can't say anything about the morning. So as of 12:00 and on, that's one thing; but as for the morning hours, from 7.00 to noon, I couldn't say anything about what he said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you hear him say after 12:00? And this is in respect to the events that you just testified about. What did you hear him say?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, Radovan Tanovic, a colleague who was killed seven days before the withdrawal, and Sladjan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were getting ready to go, and Commander Repanovic was with him. And I think he told me to join them. And then, as I've already said, I brazenly refused. I said, No, I'm not going there. Something to that effect; I can't exactly remember the words I used. And I can't also tell you what his exact words were, but I can just tell you the meaning, the intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us the meaning or the intent as you understood them.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The meaning, the essence of what was said, I've already explained, and I couldn't add anything. I just have no further answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Just for clarification, you said among the people there there was Radovan Tanovic and Sladjan Cukaric, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just trying to correct, Your Honours, what is at line 39 -- what is at line 6 at page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Correct, Sladjan Cukaric?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sladjan Cukaric and Radovan Tanovic. I know they were members of the active protective police forces. And also there was a reservist, Miroslav Petkovic. I've already said that. And that's how I see this, and I can reiterate this as many times as you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's fine. Can you recall if Cukaric was known by any other name, any -- a nickname, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sladjan Cukaric had a nickname, "Jajce." Although, when I was questioned the first time, the people who interviewed me, and I think this was on the first occasion, the 27th of February, 2003, already then they told me that his nickname was Jajce. And that's how I know it. I think he arrived in Suva Reka in January 1999 and remained there until the moment of the withdrawal of the police from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just read to you a part of the transcript of the audio recording of your interview by the war crimes judge, in which you said that -- in which you then said that Radojko Repanovic told you to go load. And I'd also like you -- the question is going to come shortly. I'd also like you to look at page 16 of your statement to the OTP in 2006. And if you could read aloud the first two sentences of paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, but the copy was also marked and highlighted. This, of course, was probably something Mr. Stamp needed, but I don't really mind the witness reading from that text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, okay, I'll read out the first two sentences as you've instructed me to do: "I did not go out with a group of police immediately but followed them after about 15 minutes. I was ordered by Repanovic to go after them and load the bodies because I had refused to kill them." He probably ordered me to do this. Somebody did order it, but you have to understand this was three years ago. This was in 2006, and three years have elapsed since, which is not a short period of time. It is possible that he was the one who had told me to go and load the dead bodies, but maybe not. But let's assume that it was him --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it that it was him who said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you if you remember who told you having seen that, and I think the sense of your answer is that you do not remember. But where was he when you were told to go and load the bodies of the people who had been killed, can you remember that? And the question is: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have two things that I can propose here, two propositions. So I can't really claim with certainty where he was. He was either in his own office or in the courtyard of the police station. He could not have been in any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You told us earlier - and I'm moving on to something else, Mr. Veljkovic - that you did not see who fired the shots at the people who were trying to escape from the Berisha family house and the environs of that house. And for the same purpose of trying to jog your memory, I'd like you to read your statement at paragraph 16 in the middle of that paragraph where you say: "... I saw a large number of people coming out of the house and running..." Can you just read that sentence and the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just find that place. Is this midway through the paragraph or midway in this statement or toward the end? I can't really find it. You are referring to paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, midway through paragraph 16, it's a rather long paragraph, but midway, approximately, you have a sentence beginning: "There I saw a large number of people coming out of the house and running..."

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it: "There I saw a large number of people coming out of the house and running away in all directions. There was a group of police officers standing outside the front of the house shooting the people as they ran away. After a short time I heard the sound of an explosion. We then walked" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd just like to read again from the same transcript of the audio recording of your testimony in Belgrade. This is page 16. The investigating judge asked you: "Did you see any people running toward the trading centre?" And you answered: "Towards the trading centre. Yes, I saw that." The investigating judge asked you: "What did you see?" And you answered: "The running -- because they entered one big house. They were locked inside, these people, as many as there were. I guess there were many. I think they were men, women, and children. And then they broke the door and entered, and when they found them there they killed some of them and some ran away and this running --" And then interrupted [sic] judge asked you: "Did you see that or not?" And you answered: "I saw them shoot. When they were running they shot." The investigating judge then asked you: "Do you know who was shooting at them?" And you said: "I know that this Tanovic was shooting a lot." And the investigating judge then asked you: "What about Jajce?" If I've got on the pronunciation correctly. Then you said: "He was a bit better than him too." The investigating judge then asked: "In what sense better?" And you answered: "He was shooting at them less than --" And the investigating judge asked: "But he was shooting as well. Was anybody else shooting?" And you said: "I think that this Miroslav Petkovic or Petrovic was shooting as well." The investigating judge then asked: "That means that they were shooting these people in the back?" And you answered: "Well, yes, as they were running. They were shooting at them running." From what I just read to you from what you said in Belgrade and also what you told the investigating officer from the OTP in 2006, can you recall now who shot these people who were running from the Berisha family house and the vicinity thereof?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was, as I've already said, audio recorded, and I was rather scared. And now as you read this, it seems funny to me how I spoke about some things. Well, first of all, you cannot see someone shooting. You can hear a shot. You can't see it. You can see a murder. And I said I saw a shot. So I really did not say it properly. I heard the shots. So those people that I mentioned, now I have some doubts. And maybe this was sinful of me, but I had to suspect that they were the ones who were shooting at these people because they had left in that direction. Now, whether all of these people whose names I mentioned shot or whether one of them just broke down the door and sent these people out and whether of the three of them only one of them shot, I'm not sure. But I suspected that it was these people who were shooting. Now, if that is incorrect, if they were not the ones who shot, then that means that my assumption was incorrect. But I had to assume that it was them because they had gone in that direction. But if my statement is incorrect, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. When you saw the people escaping from that area, from the area of the house, do you know where these policemen were, or did you see them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see these people. Because this was a big house, they were probably in the immediate vicinity, probably behind the wall, the wall of the house, and I couldn't really see them from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Let's, if we may, move on to something else quickly. You said earlier that you could not recall or that in fact you did not or nobody loaded the trucks while it drove on the Restanski Put Road. Nobody loaded the trucks with any body. Can I just refer you again to your statement and the question basically is, having read it: Does it remind you as to what you were doing with the truck as it travelled a kilometre down the Restanski Put Road? If you could go again to your statement at paragraph 16 and read the last three sentences of that paragraph aloud and slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: It probably starts with, as you are instructing me, with the words "We continued along the Restanski Put ..." Is that where you want me to read from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: "We continued along the Restanski Put passing more bodies as we went. We reached the junction with the Studencane-Pecane Road where the truck did a U-turn and then on the way back we picked up bodies on the road. When we reached the end, Ivica, the other officer and I, returned to the police station while the truck turned right and drove off in the direction of Prizren."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After the part where you said that "on the way back we picked up the bodies on the road," what is the next sentence? Can you just look at the statement. I'm asking you because on the translation I have -- there's sentence which you seem to have missed out.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the part which says: "We reached the junction with the Studencane-Pecane Road where the truck did a U-turn and then on the way back we picked up bodies on the road."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Next sentence.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: "When we reached the end, Ivica, the other police officer and I, returned to the police station while the truck turned right and drove on in the direction of Prizren." Let me clarify this a bit because I am aware of the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do that. You appear to have left out twice now a sentence that is in your statement in the English translation. Would you look again carefully in your statement. There is a sentence that finishes: "On the way back, we picked up the bodies on the road." Now, the very next sentence in your language, what does it say? From that point, read directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the last sentence: "When we reached the end, Ivica, the other officer and I" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, the point is, there is no sentence between those two. Is there any reference to a number of bodies being picked up on the road? 20 bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that sentence is not here. If you could, perhaps you could read it out and then I will have it interpreted and perhaps I can provide you with an answer concerning that particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The sentence that concerns me is: "In total there were about 20 bodies on the road."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
