utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in here. I probably did say so; it is possible. It is possible that in the course of the previous few days, people were being killed in that part, but I can't say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you say that that sentence is not in the Serbian version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, that is probably an error in the translation into the Serbian. In the copy that you signed that was read back to you, it has also the statement: "In total there were about 20 bodies on the road." You just said that you probably did say so, it is possible. My question is this: Having heard this - and that is what you said, and that is what was read back to you - can you recall what you were doing when you travelled on the road, on the Restanski Put Road, back to the Suva Reka police station? Can you recall now?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I followed the vehicle on foot; the vehicle on which the corpses of the killed Albanians were. Whether there were some additional corpses which I loaded or not, I can't say. When I was being interviewed by your colleague in Belgrade, there seems to have been a small misunderstanding regarding that. This statement of mine was hence given a different meaning. According to that translation, it seemed that I was in two different places at the same time. Your colleague asked me, Once you came back from Restanski Put Street, what happened? I said that I went to the Suva Reka police station. However, I omitted to mention the pizzeria which I explained to you. Then I nicely remember that your lady colleague simply interpreted to me what your colleague was asking me about in English, to the effect that I was not providing full answers. He asked me what was in the building. He showed me a map of Suva Reka, including the building where the people were killed, telling me that I was trying to avoid giving him a precise answer to the crucial question. And I told him, Well, I don't think you even put that question. Then he said, I did but you are trying to avoid answering it. And then I explained to him what I explained to you, i.e., what happened at the gas station and the pizzeria where the people were killed. I explained the situation in detail in five or six sentences perhaps. In the end he said, and this was interpreted to me, that he asked me that and he again repeated I was trying to avoid answering it. I simply gave up at that point because I believe that any insistence on my part could only have a negative impact. When I was in Belgrade interviewed the last time, the 4th of November last year, your presiding colleague in Belgrade, when she read the statement, asked me, How could you be in two different places the same day at the same time? This is of course impossible. I explained to her, and she was satisfied with the answer. I'm now recalling what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The bodies that you loaded in front of the Berisha family house, I think you might have said this already, but I'll ask this in case you haven't: Were they civilians, men, women, children; can you describe who these people were?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly women and children in front of the house. I already said so and I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I might be allowed to go into private session for two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your examination, does it, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed it does, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, could Mr. Stamp please provide the reference for the last question. What are the pages he was quoting from?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's page 23 in the English. It will take me some time to find the B/C/S, but I can find it and give it to counsel later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stamp. And thank you, Your Honours, for indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Veljkovic.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am a Defence team member appearing on behalf of the accused Djordjevic. My name is Djurdjic. With me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, another team member. I have a few questions of you in order to clarify some matters. Given that we speak the same language and so as to enable those interpreting to do their work properly, please wait for me to conclude my question and pause shortly before providing your answer. I will do the same.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a short break first? I need but a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are near the time for the break. May I suggest that we take the break now and then we go on until the end of the session today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will take the second break now and resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, you have explained your career. In 1999 in March, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In March 1999, were you employed at the police department in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Within that department of the interior in Suva Reka or the OUPs, as we call them, was there the police station of Suva Reka included in it?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So the OUP was at a higher level containing the police station. Who headed the OUP?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrivoje Vitosevic. I think his rank was that of a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The station commander was Mr. Repanovic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the Suva Reka OUP was within the SUP of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the Suva Reka OUP, it also comprised the OUP in Orahovac and in Dragas?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to the police station in Suva Reka within your OUP, you told us that the deputy commander was Mr. Borisavljevic and assistant was Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Mr. Borisavljevic, during the relevant time, that is to say the 26th of March, was not at work in the Suva Reka police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: You are quite right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to your duties, within your purview, that is to say the administrator of the police station, what were your tasks, administratively speaking?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the administrative part, before the terrorist attacks commenced, I usually drafted the daily work-plan. When the commander was there, I would do that together with him. When he was absent, that would probably be done with the deputy or the assistant. We would agree on any potential changes as well as the tasks issued to the beat policemen, to the patrols, and the traffic police. Mr. Repanovic made decisions and in his absence then the deputy or assistant commander. Everything would be done for the next day. I would simply go and pick up an order to execute a task which had previously been reviewed by the commander, his deputy, or assistant. In any case, one of them had to sign. I would pick up that. It would all be registered then. If there were reports, they went into the report log-book. I classified them, assigned them registered numbers, and forwarded them to any administrative clerk if needed. The person in charge always included all the addressees. Concerning any orders, I was supposed to follow up in terms of any results. If there were no results, that was even better because then it meant that the police had no work to be done. If there were results, this would be entered into the computer. And the orders were classified by types of task. Each month, I would file them in their respective files.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When the commander was there, he was issuing all of the tasks to the members of the police station; if he was absent, then it was his deputy and in turn his assistant, as you have explained?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the work-plan, did you draft any other lists?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I also registered all of the meetings. I did the same with any orders for the issuing of weapons and equipment. Then the orders would be classified by sector. If orders had been implemented, then any follow-up activities would be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically, did you keep the attendance log and did you keep or help the commander in the drafting of rosters?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of your question. Something is unclear. Just the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you keep attendance logs, those who were at work and those absent?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was all entered in the computer. It would all be done on a monthly basis. As for the reserve, force that needed to be kept by hand because the computer did not have that capacity. Only their names were in the computer but not attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about rosters?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: For the station itself, it was kept by the commander. It was kept on a monthly basis. The first and last names of the workers were entered in ball-point pen, and the working hours were entered by pencil because if there were any subsequent changes they could more easily be made. Such duty rosters until June 1998 were kept by the commander of the station. Once the terrorist attacks commenced, he simply entrusted me with keeping those lists, those rosters, under his supervision. Of course, I couldn't assign any working hours the way I pleased. I would always have to consult with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have anything to do with the daily events log?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, only the duty officer did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was entered into that log?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Any misdemeanours, disturbances of law and order, crimes, arson, traffic accidents, as well as anything else that fell within the scope of authority of the public security sector. As for the daily log, there were problems because those in the duty office were not always familiar with the type of events they had to enter. Sometimes they put in remarks which were unnecessary and sometimes they would omit things. They usually kept entries on a separate sheet of paper and then they would consult with their superior on the actual entering of items.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell me, please, what were the daily tasks of police officers at the Suva Reka police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The tasks at the police station were not the same in every police station, but they are similar. In other words, there was the duty service, the beat police, there was only one area of responsibility, as it were, for the beat police. Next there was traffic control. There was, again, just one traffic area of responsibility, and they would take care of whatever it is that it involved. Then we had the patrol duty, and they also had to keep track of their work, as well as operative operations. As for my work, it came down to oral orders. And there was nothing, there were no orders that I should issue or prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell me, please, these are the regular duties, regular tasks, up until the outbreak of the war. Now, were there any changes in the tasks after the beginning the war, let's say after the 24th?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as of June 1998, in fact, to be precise, we only had the patrol duty. The patrol shifts were eight-hour shifts, whereas the beat police duties and the traffic police no longer existed. Especially not the traffic control. It was impossible to actually conduct traffic controls because there were terrorists everywhere, so it was out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to that. Now, we've already said that the deputy was not there. Now, I would like you to clarify that a bit. Am I correct in saying that the police station, or rather, the department of the interior in Suva Reka had a PJP platoon that was part of the 5th Company -- that was part of the 5th PJP Company in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the members of the PJP unit, when there was a mission, they would go to Prizren where their tasks would be issued orally. Whereas, the rest of us remained in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So when they went to Prizren they were on different assignments and they were not registered as doing assignments in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain that. In the scheduling of tasks, they were present, but not in the mission itself. The actual work. So the commander or his deputy would tell me which people to write down as absent or on leave, on business leave, and then once that was over, once they -- their leave was over, then I would also record that in the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that as of the 26th of March, 1999, members of the PJP platoon from Suva Reka together with their commander were engaged for a mission outside the territory of Suva Reka, that they were actually with the Prizren PJP company?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Witness, do you remember that on the 25th of March, 1999, a platoon of police officers, a platoon of 30 men, let's say, was -- left the police station and went to provide security for the road in -- the communication line in Djinovci?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember where, for instance, Zoran Arizanovic, Krunoslav Jankovic, Slavoljub Jovanovic, and many other persons were -- persons who were members of the police station in Suva Reka, where they were, in other words, on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As or Zoran Arizanovic, I know that he was in the duty service. Now, whether that changed, whether his assignment changed and that did happen, I don't know. Whether he was in some different position or not, I can't recall. As for Krunoslav Jankovic that you mentioned, he was a member of the reserve forces. And as for some of the others that you also mentioned, I can't really say. I'm not sure whether they were providing security for the police station in Suva Reka, or whether they were in some other location, I really can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me where were they or where were you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- on the 25th of March, 1999, between 5.00 and 8.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you. I can't recall. Or rather, are you asking me about a.m. or p.m., 5.00 to 8.00? I think I was asleep, but I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's try and go about this in a roundabout way. Now, do you remember that food rations and water was taken by patrols, the patrol policemen, to members of the police station who were not in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. This was taken from a restaurant where the food rations were packed and then they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where the food was taken?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really recall but this would have been taken to observation posts where they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, when you mentioned the observation post, could you tell us what the observation posts were where policemen from the Suva Reka police station were assigned?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you with certainty that there was one observation post by the church, but I can't recall the complement, who exactly was in this -- at this observation post, but there were also in some other places. I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How about Siroko?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. Its possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many people were assigned to these duties; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I would say no less than three men. Maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Veljkovic, just one last thing that I would like you to clarify. The church steeple, wasn't that part of the area that was secured by the police station?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. People actually took turns and there were two-hour shifts. Most of these men who secured these posts were reserve police. Whether there were also some active duty policemen, I wouldn't know. I can't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that all the administration and everything that had to do with the reserve forces, in other words, the records, were kept by Nenad Jovanovic. Am I correct that the daily rosters, the work plans, also envisaged the activities of the reserve forces as well as the regular police forces?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that once the reservists were activated, they automatically became authorised personnel in the same manner that the regular police officers were?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say to you that when the reserve officers were activated for work at the police station, they had all the same powers as the regular police officers?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it common practice that members of the reserve force would always be accompanied by a regular police officer for these various assignments that we mentioned a little earlier, the beat police, the patrol duty, traffic police, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that members of the reserve forces provided security for the Suva Reka OUP, that that was one of their assignments?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I cannot say with certainty that it was also an assignment carried out by the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned a few moments ago the security of the station and some sacks. Now, could you tell us how the OUP station was secured and how this was done?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well this began in April 1998. Bunkers were built, constructed. So then there would be a guard who would stand guard there. There was -- he was armed with an automatic rifle, and I think there was also a machine-gun deployed there. These --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last answer. The interpreter did not understand what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. The interpreter has not been able to clearly hear and follow what you've been saying. So you were last asked up to the OUP station and how it was secured, and you answered that there was a guard who was armed with an automatic rifle and there was also a machine-gun deployed there. Now, what you said after that has not been able to be interpreted. Could you repeat the essence of what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will repeat my answer. At the guard post, there were sand sacks that were placed there in a semi-circle and the reason for that was security for the guards. Because in the event of an attack by Albanian terrorists, if fire was opened, whether from close-up, from afar, this was there to provide some sort of shelter for the guard. Shelter from small-arms fire. If not, then, of course, there would be severe consequences for the guard, but then that's something else. As for the machine-gun, it was there simply because it's effects were higher than those, and the results are better than those that you could effect with automatic rifle fire under the right conditions. If such conditions did not exist, all right, then you wouldn't use it. But this was there just as a measure of prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But I just think there was one thing that was omitted from the transcript. How many guard posts were there?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were four such posts. It's possible that there were fewer or maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there incidents involving attacks on these guard posts, and if so how many of them and how long? For how long?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for attacks, in 1998 and 1999 there were no attacks against the Suva Reka police station. However, there were some in 1997 which is the time when we were having the last periods of peace. I know that I was on leave and sometime in October 1997, I believe, my colleagues told me that there was -- had been an attack by terrorists, by attackers, who attacked the police station from the main road, the Cara Dushana Street. And according to these accounts that I heard from my colleague, they were moving in a vehicle in the direction Prizren-Pristina. They fired a number of bullets. Fortunately, none of the colleagues were either wounded or killed. Whether my colleagues at the time used their own weapons in order to prevent these men from fleeing, I don't know. But I know that there was an a investigation conducted at the time and that there were some minor damages to the facade of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there individual incidents involving attempts to shoot at the guards who were guarding these, as you call them, bunkers?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not against the men who were at the police station working for the police station. As for the special units, the PJP units, I really wouldn't know about that, and I couldn't go into that. But as far as the men who were members of the police station were, there were no such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not sure that you understood my question properly. I don't mean were there any attacks against the police station itself; but against the guards, the individual guards?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any. When you said individual guards, I automatically understood that to mean also the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, how were these men who went on patrols, how were -- what kind of equipment did they have with them, and what kind of uniforms did they have on?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: They had blue camouflage uniforms, and they were fully armed with automatic rifles, four clips of rounds. They went and patrolled certain areas. I don't know if they elected to do so or were ordered to do so, but that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was this the case in 1997 and 1998? Was that the standard procedure that they would go out equipped like that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ever since the terrorist attacks began, that was their standard equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us when these terrorist attacks started, and what did they involve as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: There were -- there had always been incidents involving shooting at members of the police in Kosovo. However, beginning in March, March 1st, 1998, when the terrorists rebelled, then it became an every-day occurrence, and people had to go on patrols, which they didn't really like, but they had no choice, they had to go, because nobody really wanted to know whether they would get killed there or not. Anyway, they had to go. So this started in March 1998 and it went on until our withdrawal in 1999, when we had no respite whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any attacks on civilians who were not of Albanian ethnicity as well as on those Albanians who were loyal to the Republic of Serbia? Were there any kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think in April 1998. That is when the Albanian terrorists started killing those who refused to join the KLA. They did not kill Serbs at the outset. I remember a person who came to the station who provided information on the people who possessed arms illegally. In April or May 1999, I heard that he was found dead somewhere around the village of Restane. He was killed next to the road. His throat was slit. As for any kidnappings, in June, 1999, in mid-June, within two or three days, some Serb civilians were kidnapped by the Albanian terrorists. The fate of those people is still unknown. Among them was a work-mate, Miodrag Krstic who arrived some three weeks -- who left work three weeks before he was kidnapped. He simply applied to be dismissed. After that, he was ill. He went to Belgrade with his brother. And upon his return, he was kidnapped. His fate is still unknown. As is that of his brother as well as some other people who were kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, I lack discipline and yet I still have to warn you to speak more slowly so that the interpreters could interpret everything you say and that it be translated into the transcript. Hence, can you speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat my last answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think everything is in the transcript concerning my last question. Just slow down a bit. In the territory of Suva Reka, there is a number of villages. You mentioned, among others, Restane; Djinovci -- sorry, not Djinovci, Budakovo; Belance; et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Blace, not Belance. It's Belanica or Blace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could the police go there on patrol as of the summer of 1998 onwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, as of that point they no longer went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: For their personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on the police patrols moving about that area?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was certain danger and the people were simply not being sent there anymore. They could not mount any attacks on the police if the police were not present. There was a lot of danger there because these were ethnically purely Albanian villages. No one wanted to send them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In Suva Reka itself, were there any attacks such as the attack on Milorad Nisavic in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am very well familiar with that event, I think it was June 1998, in the morning between 8.30 and 9.00. My colleagues and I returned from breakfast. And just as I entered the auxiliary building where I was supposed to start work, one could hear a lot of firing in Suva Reka from the direction of Prizren. There was a group of people firing and there seemed to have been one person responding. And I thought to myself, Here comes a war. However, that only lasted briefly. Perhaps five or six seconds. Two minutes later, people rushed in and a work-mate said, Look, Milorad, or Debeljko [phoen] as we called him, was wounded. When I saw him, his entire left side of the body was covered in blood and I said, He was hit in the stomach. But then I thought that had he been hit in the stomach, he would not have been able to walk. Later on, it turned out he was wounded in the left arm. As he was getting out of the vehicle at the bridge where there was a newspaper stand and having wanted to get a newspaper, he was sprayed with bullets from across the road. As he was approaching the stand to buy that newspaper, the attackers opened fire. I don't know how many there were. Thanks to his composure and skill, he managed to return fire. In any case, he was seriously wounded in that attack. However, the person working at the stand who was Albanian was killed on the spot. Milorad Nisavic was taken to the health clinic and then transferred to Prizren. He spent over half a year there. First one and a half months in hospital and then on treatment. He returned to work just prior to the bombardment. He subsequently told us that he could recognise those who opened fire on him from some 7 or 8 metres. They wore no masks. Of course, we couldn't tell him, No, it was impossible for you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the station compound, you had a building which served as a dorm. As of the summer of 1998, could you walk around Suva Reka, especially its outer parts?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That would be putting up a challenge to your own fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: To walk around at night on the street when there are terrorist attacks? I can't call it anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Veljkovic, did you know that there were traffic check-points along the main roads?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was only patrolling and preventive checks, but I don't think there was such a thing as official check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the police station of Suva Reka itself, but did you travel on different roads in Kosovo and Metohija? Did you come across check-points where traffic checks were carried out?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some, for example, in Stimlje and in the territory of Suva Reka as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that all vehicles that would come upon such a check-point would be checked irrespective who the driver was or what the vehicle was, all vehicles were checked?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Only individual vehicles. This was a major road with dense traffic, therefore not all vehicles could be stopped. You would create bottlenecks resulting in columns of vehicles. Only individual vehicles were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was this done in order to locate any weapons or other illegal objects that may be found in such vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As of the beginning of the attacks, it was done preventively, exclusively for that reason, to see whether someone was a terrorist, whether there was any arms and munitions smuggling. That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Looking at the registration plate on a vehicle, can you tell who that vehicle belongs to?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to what person? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you sigh a vehicle approaching with registration plates.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Of course you could tell an official vehicle apart with police plates, but if the vehicle has civilian plates then you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any attacks in January 1999 -- sorry, let me ask you something else. In the summer of 1998, do you recall whether any roads were blocked such as between Pristina and Suva Reka at Duljenje [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think, yes. As of June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit D002-4026. Can we zoom in on the central part of the map, please. Could we please go down a bit, a bit more. So that we have Pristina on the top. I can't see Prizren. There. A little bit more to see the lower part of the Prizren area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljkovic, if one goes from Suva Reka via Dulje and Stimlje to Pristina, how many kilometres is that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I never measured that but my work-mates told me that it's about 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And once the road was blocked, you had to go through Prizren via Sredacka Zupa and Strpce to reach the road between Skopje and Pristina to turn towards Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How much longer did one have to travel that route?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: By an hour or an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that lasted for almost three months?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Until September 1998. Once the road between Prizren and Pristina was deblocked, then for a short while vehicles could move. But as of December and January when even fiercer terrorist attacks began on the police, then that ceased as well. And one still had to go via Brezovica or the route you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Veljkovic, in July 1998, as far as Orahovac, Zociste, and Velika Hoca, and Retimlje were concerned, do you remember that the KLA occupied those settlements?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that. I did not participate in those operations. I can't give you any details, but I do know about that since some of my work-mates went there. Orahovac was under attack, the very centre of town, and people were kidnapped from their homes and executed. Some of my colleagues were seriously injured and some killed. That lasted for about two or three days, I think. This is as far as any knowledge of mine goes, since I didn't participate in those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that. But can you tell us anything that would be interesting for the Chamber to hear and that you had heard from your work-mates who were there? If you have any additional details that were shared with you.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing more. These were quite bad events which did not deserve any additional questions. I didn't ask. All of them basically said the same story, that any patrolling would be flirting with death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Until the war began, how many officers from the police station in Suva Reka were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR VELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the beginning of the war, I know of three colleagues who were killed. I also know that there was a number of them who were lightly or gravely injured. I do know for certain that the three were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Defence document D0024-2254 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, and with respect to my friend, I see he is moving on to something else. And I am wondering if, having regard to the time, we could do that tomorrow. And I could spend the last two minutes raising an issue of scheduling and asking for the guidance of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time for you, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully support my learned friend Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I point out before we move from the evidence, Mr. Djurdjic, that we have heard a very great deal about events, particularly in 1998 to date in your cross-examination. The events we are concerned with are events that occurred essentially in March of 1999 with this witness. And we had hoped that tomorrow you may be able to focus on those because there are other witnesses we need to deal with this week. We must adjourn shortly so that we will continue tomorrow at 9.00. The Court Officer will show you out now. We have to deal with a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just rose to mention that on Friday we have scheduled Ambassador Knut Vollebaek who at this point in time has an extraordinarily tough schedule and he asked that he be completed that day. Otherwise it will be very difficult to get him back here within the near future. After this witness, we have scheduled Mr. Phillip Coo. And subject to the Court, I was wondering if either we break Mr. Coo's testimony if he is not completed by Friday and interpose Ambassador Vollebaek on Friday, or if perhaps after this witness, we reschedule Mr. Coo to be the next witness immediately after Ambassador Vollebaek. And I'm now reminded that we have the videolink issue next week, so there is some difficulty. But I think Mr. Coo is flexible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When are the videolinks planned next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, and if not completed, on Thursday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many witnesses is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So far three. We think they could be done in two days and we hope that the Court might look kindly upon our application to add a fourth. But we think that if there are four, we could do them in three days at the most. They are all crime-based witnesses under rules 92 ter or 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a growing tendency for time slippage which the Chamber is going to become more concerned about. I mention that as a general proposition because it seems to me that with respect to the videolinks next week if there is proper discipline by counsel, it ought to be possible to deal with the three witnesses presently listed in two days, Monday and Tuesday. I'm not in a position to tell you whether there will be an additional witness or not at this point. With respect to this week, Mr. Stamp, this witness presently before us ought to be completed well in the course of tomorrow. And I would expect that we can then, if you haven't a short witness available, commence the evidence of Mr. Coo. The Ambassador can be interrupted in the course of the evidence of Mr. Coo, and his evidence should not take the full day so that we can on Friday presumably return to evidence of Mr. Coo. Now, whether we will complete Mr. Coo before the videolink I think is ambitious, so that it is likely that you are going to have to arrange with Mr. Coo to be available next week when the videolinks come to an end. We can't, at this moment, estimate when that will be, but you will be able to maintain liaison with him about timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I will be guided by that and proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I mention that in the week following, as I've mentioned to counsel, we are not going to sit on the Thursday and Friday to allow people to return for the vacation. On the Wednesday, which will be the last sitting day, there is a Plenary in the morning. And for that reason, we will not be able to commence until later in the day. And it is presently planned that we will sit from 1.30 until 4.30. The courtroom is required at 4.30 for another matter, so we will have to conclude our hearing on that day by 4.30. But to enable that, we will commence at 1.30 rather than the 2.15 which would be the normal time. Is there another matter, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be brief, Your Honours. If I understood my colleague Mr. Stamp correctly, he informed us a while ago, and we accepted that, that Mr. Vollebaek has to come on Friday to testify and that his testimony should be completed on Friday. We are aware of that. As for Mr. Coo, I don't know if there will be enough time to hear him, but I understand that the Prosecutor can bring him at any point in time and that he is flexible. But I do not understand the videolink part. On the original list we had two witnesses proposed and now there is another witness being proposed here and we object to that witness testifying via videolink. Of course, depending on the decision by the Trial Chamber, that might be three as well. But as for the fourth witness, which is at issue here, he has never been a witness before the ICTY before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, will you please liaise with Mr. Djurdjic as to the witnesses that are the subject of present orders for videolink and as to the additional witness that you propose so that Mr. Djurdjic is well aware of the witnesses presently ordered and the possibility of a further one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of July 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
